Evaluation of postfix expression using stack
2: Insertion and deletion to/from Linked Lists

questions.q: Explain the time-space trade-off with one example from data structures.
questions.model: Using more memory can reduce running time and vice versa. Example: a hash table uses extra space to give average O(1) search instead of O(n) linear search; a lookup table of precomputed values trades memory for speed.

questions.t: Conversion of Infix to Prefix and Postfix Expressions
questions.q: Convert the infix expression A + B * (C - D) / E to postfix using a stack, showing the stack contents after each symbol.
questions.model: Postfix: A B C D - * E / +. Operators are pushed by precedence; '(' is pushed, ')' pops to '('; '*' and '/' (left-associative) pop each other before '+' is popped at the end.

questions.t: Evaluation of postfix expression using stack
questions.q: Evaluate the postfix expression 6 2 3 + - 3 8 2 / + * using a stack.
How many disk moves does the recursive solution of the Tower of Hanoi make for 7 disks?

A 1000 x 1000 matrix of integers has only 2000 non-zero entries. Compare the memory needed by a 2D array and by a triplet (row, column, value) representation, assuming 4-byte integers, and state which you would use.
questions.model: 2D array: 10^6 x 4 = 4,000,000 bytes. Triplets: 2000 x 3 x 4 = 24,000 bytes (plus a header row). The triplet form uses about 0.6% of the memory, so it is preferred for sparse data.

questions.q: In an array-based circular queue of size N that keeps one slot empty, which condition indicates the queue is full?
questions.model: With one slot left empty, the queue is full when advancing rear would reach front: (rear + 1) % N == front.

questions.t: Insertion and deletion to/from Linked Lists
questions.q: Write a C function that deletes the first node with a given key from a singly linked list and returns the (possibly new) head. Handle the empty list and deletion of the head node.
Read the assertion and reason about doubly linked list and choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Given a pointer to a node, deleting that node takes O(1) time in a doubly linked list.
questions.reason: Each node of a doubly linked list stores a pointer to its predecessor as well as its successor.
questions.model: Both true and R explains A: the predecessor is reachable directly, so no traversal is needed.

questions.q: A hospital triage system must always serve the most critical patient first while patients keep arriving. Evaluate a sorted linked list and a binary heap as implementations of this priority queue and recommend one.
questions.model: Sorted list: insert O(n), remove-max O(1). Binary heap: insert and remove-max O(log n). With frequent arrivals and removals the heap's O(log n) for both operations is better overall, so recommend the heap.

questions.q: The preorder traversal of a binary tree is A B D E C F and its inorder traversal is D B E A F C. Construct the tree and give its postorder traversal.
questions.model: Root A; left subtree from inorder D B E (root B, children D and E); right subtree F C (root C, left child F). Postorder: D E B F C A.

questions.q: Build a Huffman tree for symbols with frequencies a:5, b:9, c:12, d:13, e:16, f:45. What is the total number of bits needed to encode a message with exactly these frequencies?
What is the maximum number of comparisons binary search needs to find a key in a sorted array of 1000 elements?
questions.model: ceil(log2(1001)) = 10 comparisons in the worst case.

questions.q: Insert the keys 23, 43, 13, 27 into a hash table of size 10 using h(k) = k mod 10 with (a) linear probing and (b) separate chaining. Show both tables and compare the two strategies for clustering and memory use.
questions.model: h: 23->3, 43->3, 13->3, 27->7. Linear probing: 23 at 3, 43 at 4, 13 at 5, 27 at 7 (primary clustering at 3-5). Chaining: slot 3 holds 23 -> 43 -> 13, slot 7 holds 27. Chaining avoids clustering but needs extra pointer memory; probing stores keys in the table but degrades as load factor rises.

questions.q: Explain why quick sort with the first element as pivot takes O(n^2) time on an already sorted array, and suggest a pivot strategy that avoids it.
questions.model: Each partition splits off only the pivot, giving partitions of size n-1, n-2, ...: n(n-1)/2 comparisons. Choosing a random pivot or median-of-three gives balanced partitions on average, O(n log n).

questions.q: True or False: Two-way merge sort takes O(n log n) time in the best, average and worst cases.
questions.model: True: it always splits in halves (log n levels) and merges n elements per level.

questions.q: Insert the keys 30, 20, 10, 25, 28, 40 one by one into an empty AVL tree. Show the tree after each insertion and name each rotation performed.
questions.model: 30,20,10: LL imbalance at 30 -> right rotation, root 20 (10, 30). 25: under 30's left. 28: LR imbalance at 30 -> left rotation at 25 then right rotation at 30, giving 28 with children 25 and 30. 40: right child of 30, which makes the root 20 unbalanced (left height 1, right height 3, RR case) -> left rotation at 20. Final: 28 with left subtree 20 (10, 25) and right subtree 30 (-, 40).

questions.q: Heap sort first builds a ___ heap in O(n) time and then repeatedly swaps the root with the last element, giving an overall worst-case time of ___.
questions.model: A max-heap is built, then n extract steps of O(log n): O(n log n).

questions.q: Explain why B+ tree index files are preferred over B tree index files for range queries on a database file.
questions.model: In a B+ tree all records (or pointers) are in the leaves, which are linked in key order; a range query finds the first key and scans the leaf chain. In a B tree keys are spread over internal nodes, requiring tree traversal for a range.

questions.q: A graph has vertices 1-6 and edges 1-2, 1-3, 2-4, 2-5, 3-5, 5-6, with adjacency lists in increasing order. Give the BFS and DFS orders starting from vertex 1 and name the data structure each traversal uses.
questions.model: BFS (queue): 1 2 3 4 5 6. DFS (stack/recursion): 1 2 4 5 3 6. BFS visits level by level; DFS goes deep along 1-2-4, backtracks to 5, then 3 and 6.

questions.q: Model the case as a weighted graph, find a minimum spanning tree with Kruskal's or Prim's algorithm, and state its total cost. Explain which data structures make your chosen algorithm efficient.
questions.case: A campus must connect five buildings A, B, C, D and E with fibre. Cable costs (in lakh rupees) are: A-B 4, A-C 3, B-C 1, B-D 2, C-D 4, C-E 5, D-E 6. Every building must be reachable and the total cost must be minimum.
questions.model: Kruskal: B-C 1, B-D 2, A-C 3, then C-E 5 (A-B 4 and C-D 4 form cycles). MST cost = 1 + 2 + 3 + 5 = 11 lakh. Kruskal uses sorting plus a union-find (disjoint set) structure; Prim uses a priority queue (heap).
